design_detail: Single-site, open-label, single-group pilot trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05979844; protocol published as Morland et al., 2024) at the VA San Diego Healthcare System: eight US military veterans with PTSD (CAPS-5 of 28 or more) and their intimate partners (N = 16), recruited September 2023 to March 2025, received an eight-session brief cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy (bCBCT) with an MDMA preparation session, two full-day MDMA sessions for the veteran only (the partner joined for the last 1 to 2 hours) and dyadic integration sessions drawing on integrative behavioral couple therapy, over about 7 weeks; assessments at baseline, mid-treatment, end of treatment and 3 and 6 months after. bCBCT sessions were delivered by video; MDMA sessions in person at the VA hospital. Funded by the Heroic Hearts Project; MDMA supplied by Resilient Pharmaceuticals (formerly Lykos Therapeutics). Published online 4 September 2026 (Early View). The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, appraised with ROBINS-I.
can_establish: That a brief conjoint therapy with two MDMA sessions for the veteran alone could be delivered within a VA health system to eight couples, all of whom completed it, and what happened to PTSD symptoms, relationship satisfaction and adverse events over 6 months in these 16 people.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA added anything to bCBCT, which the authors' own earlier trial found effective without MDMA, or whether dosing only the veteran preserves any relational benefit (there is no comparison arm of any kind); durability (PTSD and relationship scores partly rebounded); rare harms; or effects in couples with intimate partner violence, severe aggression, current serious suicide risk or substance use needing detoxification, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Referred from VA mental health clinics or self-referred within the VA San Diego Healthcare System; 105 referrals (59 from providers, 46 self-referrals), 85 screened in some way, eight couples enrolled (METHOD › Participants, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 note; RESULTS › Feasibility and acceptability, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Veterans: DSM-5 PTSD on the CAPS-5 with a total severity of at least 28; partners: in a committed relationship, willing to take part, PCL-5 of 30 or less; both 18 or older, agreeing to lifestyle restrictions including medication rules and no other trauma- or couple-focused therapy. Excluded: panic disorder, bipolar and psychotic disorders, current serious suicide risk (C-SSRS 4 or more weekly or any suicidal behaviour within 6 months), intimate partner violence, severe relationship aggression, alcohol or substance use involving withdrawal or needing detoxification or judged a safety concern; uncontrolled hypertension, cardiovascular or neurovascular disease or other unstable conditions. Full abstinence was not required, but a plan to reduce alcohol and substance use was (METHOD › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Veterans: mean age 45.57 (range 28 to 60); 5 men; 7 heterosexual; 5 White, the rest Asian or another race; 2 Hispanic or Latino; 3 taking psychoactive medicines; 6 with one or more past or current comorbidities including major depressive disorder and substance use disorders. Partners: mean age 42.50 (30 to 55); 3 men; all heterosexual; 6 White. Mostly married; mean relationship length 14.88 years (2 to 34); median household income above $105,000 (METHOD › Participants, 3rd paragraph).
sample.attrition: All couples completed every MDMA and bCBCT session; two partners missed the 3-month follow-up but completed the 6-month one (RESULTS › Feasibility and acceptability; Fig. 2 note; Data analysis, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteer veteran couples within one VA system, with relatively high income and education; couples with violence or severe aggression excluded. Expectations of MDMA treatment were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: bCBCT sessions 1 to 3 in one 4-hour session and 4 to 5 in one 3-hour session, an MDMA preparation session (1.5 hours) the business day before the first MDMA session (6 to 8 hours), an integration session the next day, bCBCT sessions 6 and 7 over 2 weeks, the second MDMA session the week after session 7, a second integration session the next morning and the last bCBCT session about a week later; up to three further integration sessions as needed; a primary therapist at every session and a co-therapist at the preparation, MDMA and integration sessions; 92% adherence to the manual in a 10% sample of sessions (METHOD › Treatment, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Treatment and assessment fidelity and reliability monitoring, 1st paragraph). Before each MDMA session: breathalyser, urine pregnancy and drug tests and vital signs (Treatment delivery › Treatment modality, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed, for the veteran only: 80 mg MDMA HCl (about 68 mg MDMA) with an optional supplemental 40 mg MDMA HCl (about 34 mg) in the first session, and 100 mg MDMA HCl (about 84 mg) with an optional supplemental 40 mg MDMA HCl in the second; by mouth is implied, not stated; partners received no MDMA (METHOD › Treatment, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Full abstinence from alcohol and other drugs was not required, only an agreed plan to reduce use (METHOD › Participants, 2nd paragraph). One veteran had a urine test positive for cocaine before the second MDMA session, which was cancelled and rescheduled; the same participant used trazodone infrequently by misunderstanding (RESULTS › Safety › Medication management, 1st paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; antidepressants were tapered before treatment (three veterans).

comparison.controls: None: within-person change from baseline to end of treatment and from end of treatment to 6 months.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; bCBCT itself (effective without MDMA in the authors' earlier trial), time, regression to the mean and expectation are uncontrolled.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: CAPS-5 (virtual interviews by trained bachelor's- and graduate-level assessors; 35% of interviews double-rated, ICC .99), with treatment response (a fall of at least 12 points), loss of diagnosis and remission (end-of-treatment score below 12). Secondary: Couple Satisfaction Index (CSI-32; distress below 104.5; reliable change 13.61 points in this sample), PCL-5 and its collateral version for partners, Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8). Safety: adverse events, adverse events of special interest (cardiac, suicide risk, abuse potential), treatment-emergent and serious adverse events, vital signs before the first and supplemental doses and at the end of sessions, C-SSRS before every session (METHOD › Measures, all subsections; Treatment and assessment fidelity and reliability monitoring, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated measures with sample alphas reported (CAPS-5 .86; CSI-32 .97 and .98; PCL-C .88; CSQ-8 .96).
outcomes.operationalization: Cohen's d from estimated marginal means of piecewise linear models (treatment segment: baseline, mid-treatment, end of treatment; follow-up segment: end of treatment, 3 and 6 months) that controlled for baseline levels; dyadic two-intercept models for relationship satisfaction; reliable and clinically significant change by Jacobson and Truax (Data analysis, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no significance tests; effect sizes and categories of change are reported for CAPS-5, CSI-32 (veterans and partners), PCL-5, PCL-C and CSQ-8. PCL-5 and PCL-C results are not reported in the text.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open-label; the CAPS-5 assessors are not described as blind and all veterans had received MDMA; relationship and satisfaction outcomes are self-reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: CAPS-5: baseline 39.13 (SD 10.56), range 29 to 55; treatment period d = −1.25; mean fall 16.1 points (SD 11.4; range 3 to 34); response 5 of 8 (62.5%), loss of diagnosis 3 of 8 (37.5%), remission 2 of 8 (25.0%); follow-up rebound of 6.3 points, d = 0.29 (RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 note). CSI-32: treatment period d = 1.83 for veterans and 1.29 for partners, mean rise 27.9 (SD 31.8) and 19.8 (23.1); follow-up rebound d = −0.68 and −0.47; reliable improvement in 5 veterans and 5 partners (10 of 16), reliable deterioration in 1 partner (a fall of 16 points) (RESULTS › Relationship satisfaction, 1st paragraph). Editors' arithmetic: the two printed mean changes imply a net fall of about 10 CAPS-5 points from baseline to 6 months (16.1 − 6.3); the printed d of −1.25 is smaller than the raw mean change divided by its SD (1.41) or by the baseline SD (1.52), because it comes from baseline-adjusted model estimates.
analysis.covariates: Baseline level of each outcome in the piecewise models (Data analysis, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05979844: first submitted 31 July 2023, posted 7 August 2023, before the actual start (6 October 2023); single-group, open-label; enrollment 16; phase given as 3. Registered primary outcome: clinician-rated PTSD symptoms from baseline to 6 months after treatment; secondary: relationship satisfaction over the same period; no results posted; collaborators Healing Breakthrough, Resilient Pharmaceuticals and the VA San Diego Healthcare System (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17). The article reports the change to the end of treatment as its main effect and the follow-up as a rebound, without a single baseline-to-6-month estimate.
analysis.selective_reporting: PCL-5 and PCL-C (secondary endpoints) are named but their results are not given in the text; vital signs and the full adverse-event list are in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 (downloads, not read).
analysis.power: No power calculation; a pilot of eight couples.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In eight veteran couples, veterans' CAPS-5 scores fell by 16 points on average during a 7-week brief couple therapy with two MDMA sessions for the veteran (5 responders, 3 who lost the diagnosis, 2 in remission), then rose again by about 6 points by 6 months; relationship satisfaction rose for both partners and partly fell back; one partner's satisfaction worsened. All couples completed, there were no serious adverse events, every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, and one had a cocaine-positive urine test before a session. Nothing in the design can attribute these changes to MDMA, and the authors note that the rates of loss of diagnosis and remission were close to those of bCBCT without MDMA in the same population.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes preliminary evidence of potential improvements with no identified serious safety concerns, and the summary says the treatment "was associated with large improvements" (Abstract; DISCUSSION, 8th paragraph). Elsewhere the Discussion says the study provides preliminary evidence that the treatment is safe and can yield clinically meaningful improvements when only the veteran receives MDMA, that MDMA's therapeutic effects may generalize across delivery formats, and that dosing only the partner with PTSD can preserve relational benefit while potentially reducing medical risk (DISCUSSION, 1st to 3rd paragraphs): comparative statements that the single-arm design cannot support. The Limitations say the open-label design, small sample and lack of a comparison condition preclude causal inference (DISCUSSION, 7th paragraph).

timeline.event: Monson et al., Eur J Psychotraumatol: six couples, full CBCT with both partners dosed (uncontrolled); Anne C. Wagner is an author of both studies.
Morland et al., Contemp Clin Trials Commun: this study's protocol (on the project's evidence map; not read).
This pilot: eight veteran couples, brief CBCT with only the veteran dosed (uncontrolled).

replication.where_it_stands: Two small uncontrolled studies of MDMA with conjoint therapy, sharing an author and with different protocols; the project's evidence map lists a registered randomized trial of conjoint therapy with and without MDMA (NCT06044675, recruiting). No controlled result exists in the sources read.

funding.funder: A grant from the Heroic Hearts Project; the investigational product was supplied by Resilient Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (formerly Lykos Therapeutics); Kayla Knopp and Chandra Khalifian were supported by VA Rehabilitation Research & Development career development awards (RC003777, RX003490) (AUTHOR NOTE).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Christopher Stauffer reports funding grants from the Steven & Alexandra Cohen Foundation and the Dr. Bronner Family Foundation; the authors have no other conflicts (AUTHOR NOTE).
funding.affiliations_note: VA investigators; the principal investigator developed the brief CBCT protocol in an earlier trial (Introduction, 2nd paragraph). The registry names the principal investigator as sponsor and Resilient Pharmaceuticals among collaborators. Data available on written request (OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in veteran couples comparing brief CBCT with MDMA for the veteran against the same therapy with an active placebo, with blinded assessors, measured expectancy, registered 6-month outcomes and enough couples to estimate relational effects.

domains.note: No comparison group; the package includes bCBCT, which improved PTSD without MDMA in the authors' earlier trial, so no change can be attributed to MDMA.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteer couples from one VA system; violence and severe aggression excluded.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Variable numbers of optional integration sessions; one veteran's second MDMA session was rescheduled after a cocaine-positive test and the same veteran used trazodone; antidepressants were tapered before treatment.
All completed treatment; two partners missed one follow-up, handled by maximum likelihood.
Open-label: CAPS-5 assessors not described as blind, and relationship outcomes self-reported by couples who knew the veteran had taken MDMA.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Prospectively registered, but the registered time frame (baseline to 6 months) is not reported as one estimate, PCL-5 results are not given, and effect sizes come from baseline-adjusted models whose standardizer is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that MDMA improves PTSD or relationships when added to brief conjoint therapy, the study is at critical risk of bias: there is no comparison arm and the base therapy is itself effective. Unblinded outcomes add serious concerns. It can be cited for feasibility in a VA setting, for the observed changes and rebound in eight couples, and for the adverse events seen; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for the benefit of dosing only one partner, or for rare harms.

key_findings.finding: Eight veterans with PTSD and their partners (N = 16) from 105 referrals; veterans mean age 45.57 (28 to 60), 5 men, 5 White, 3 taking psychoactive medicines, 6 with past or current comorbidities; partners mean age 42.50, 3 men, all heterosexual; mean relationship length 14.88 years.
key_findings.locator: METHOD › Participants, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Fig. 2 note

key_findings.finding: PTSD (CAPS-5): baseline mean 39.13 (SD 10.56; range 29 to 55); during treatment d = −1.25, with a mean fall of 16.1 points (SD 11.4; range 3 to 34); response in 5 of 8 (62.5%), loss of diagnosis in 3 (37.5%), remission in 2 (25.0%); small rebound during follow-up (mean 6.3 points, d = 0.29).
key_findings.locator: RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 note
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: a net fall of about 10 points from baseline to 6 months; the printed d comes from baseline-adjusted model estimates and is smaller than the raw mean change divided by its SD (1.41).

key_findings.finding: Relationship satisfaction (CSI-32): during treatment d = 1.83 for veterans and 1.29 for partners (mean rise 27.9, SD 31.8, and 19.8, SD 23.1); rebound during follow-up d = −0.68 and −0.47; reliable improvement in 5 veterans and 5 partners (10 of 16), reliable deterioration in 1 partner (a fall of 16 points); 4 of 6 distressed veterans and 4 of 6 distressed partners moved out of the distressed range, and one partner moved into it.
key_findings.locator: RESULTS › Relationship satisfaction, 1st paragraph; Fig. 4 note

key_findings.finding: Only 50.0% of veterans and 50.0% of partners showed both reliable and clinically significant improvement in relationship satisfaction.

Safety: no serious adverse events; every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; transient rises in blood pressure and pulse in sessions (values only in Supplementary Table S1, not read); events in more than one participant within 7 days of an MDMA session: headache 75.0% (6 of 8), feeling warm or hot 37.5%, increased blood pressure 37.5%, nausea 25.0%, decreased appetite 25.0%, sadness 25.0%.

Suicidality: no high-risk responses on the C-SSRS; one participant developed active ideation without plan or intent during the pre-treatment medication taper and reported passive ideation after each MDMA session; one participant's passive ideation became active during follow-up, alongside a bereavement unrelated to the study; two with passive ideation at baseline did not worsen.

Medication and drug use: three veterans tapered off antidepressants (duloxetine, paroxetine, desvenlafaxine) before treatment without dropout; one paused a stimulant for ADHD before each MDMA session; one had a urine test positive for cocaine before the second MDMA session (an adverse event of special interest), which was cancelled and rescheduled, and also used trazodone infrequently.
Feasibility: all couples completed every MDMA and bCBCT session; treatment satisfaction (CSQ-8, out of 4) 3.77 (SD 0.27) for veterans and 3.81 (0.34) for partners.

Rates of loss of diagnosis (37.5%) and remission (25%) were lower than in the two phase 3 MDMA trials (67% and 33%; 71.2% and 46.2%) and, the authors say, closer to those of bCBCT without MDMA in the same population (Morland et al., 2022).

Registration: NCT05979844 first submitted 31 July 2023 and posted 7 August 2023, before the start on 6 October 2023; single group, open-label, enrollment 16, phase given as 3; primary outcome clinician-rated PTSD symptoms from baseline to 6 months after treatment, secondary relationship satisfaction over the same period; no results posted.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05979844 (API v2) › Status; Design; Outcome Measures

key_findings.finding: Funding: Heroic Hearts Project grant; MDMA supplied by Resilient Pharmaceuticals (formerly Lykos Therapeutics); VA career development awards for two authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The account of relational distress is incomplete and ambiguous: six of eight veterans and six of eight partners are said to have been distressed at baseline and four of each to have improved clinically; the next sentence, about 'the remaining two veterans and one of the remaining partners', describes people who began and stayed nondistressed, and the last partner is said to have begun nondistressed and deteriorated. What happened to the two distressed veterans and two distressed partners who did not improve clinically is not stated, and 'remaining' reads as if it referred to them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Presumably those four stayed distressed, but the text does not say; cite the reliable-change counts and the four of six who improved.

reporting_issues.issue: Treatment-emergent adverse events are defined as events during or within 2 days after MDMA administration (Methods), but the most frequent ones are reported as those within 7 days of an MDMA session (Results).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (METHOD › Measures › Safety endpoints › Adverse event tracking; RESULTS › Safety › AEs, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The window behind the reported percentages is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered primary time frame is baseline to 6 months after treatment, but the article reports the change to the end of treatment as its main effect and the follow-up only as a rebound; the PCL-5 and PCL-C results, named as secondary endpoints, are not given; the registry calls this open-label pilot phase 3.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Design; Outcome Measures); publisher HTML (METHOD › Measures; RESULTS)
reporting_issues.consequence: The registered outcome has to be reconstructed (about a 10-point net fall, editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: Effect sizes come from estimated marginal means of models that controlled for baseline levels of each outcome, a within-group change model; the standardizer is not stated, and the printed d for CAPS-5 (−1.25) cannot be reproduced from the printed raw change (16.1, SD 11.4) or baseline SD (10.56).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Data analysis, 1st paragraph; RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the raw changes and counts rather than the d values.
